notes: West leads the ♠8 against 3NT. West's lead is won by South with the ♠J. There are 7 top tricks (the spade trick just won, 3 hearts, 2 diamonds, and the ♣A). South should try to develop 2 extra tricks in diamonds.

For this to be possible, diamonds must be 3-3. A diamond trick will have to be lost and South should gear his play towards losing that trick to West. Should East gain the lead in diamonds, the defense may be in a position to take 4 spade tricks.

South should cross to the dummy in hearts and lead a diamond towards his hand. If East follows with the ♦7, the lowest outstanding diamond, South ducks and West must win the trick. The contract is safe as West cannot attack spades profitably from his side of the table.

If East plays a diamond other than the ♦7, South wins the trick and crosses again in hearts. Dummy's other diamond is played, South ducking as before if East plays the ♦7. If East does not play the ♦7, South wins and plays a third round. As long as East started with the ♦7 (and the suit is 3-3), West will have to win this trick) and the contract will be safe.

If West follows small the trick is won in dummy. A diamond trick is now conceded. If West was dealt the ♦Q he will be forced to win the trick. As long as diamonds are 3-3 the contract will be safe. The ♥K will be an entry to the long diamonds in dummy.

This deal looks superficially similar to the last one (C-1). Both deals involve establishing the diamond suit for 4 tricks. In this deal, South must play to keep the defender to the right of the long suit off lead. If South wins the opening heart lead with the ♥A and cashes the top diamonds, a 3-1 diamond break will doom the contract. The diamond blockage will allow South to cash only 1 of the 2 remaining diamond tricks.
South can guard against a 3-1 diamond break by ducking the opening lead in dummy. West must continue hearts to knock out dummy's side entry, but South should duck again.

If West switches at trick 3, South can cross in diamonds and discard a diamond on the ♥A. Once again the diamond suit will provide 5 cashable tricks.

Dummy's diamonds will provide enough discards for South's spade and club losers. There is a certain loser in the trump suit, however, and that suit must be 3-2 for the contract to have a chance.

South should try to arrange to run dummy's diamonds after drawing all of the outstanding trumps. South should begin by cashing the ♦A. The diamond suit can now be run in comfort.

Notice that it is inferior to duck the first round of trump after cashing the ♦A. If one of the defenders started with a doubleton heart and a singleton club, the defense would be able to take a club ruff. Winning a round of trump before ducking a round effectively guards against this possibility.

South will need to depend on the diamond finesse. East will have to have the ♦K. If East has a doubleton ♦K, South must play a low diamond to the ♦J and cash the ♦A on the second round. If East has 4 diamonds it will be necessary to assume that West has a doubleton ♦10. In this case, the ♦Q will have to be played on the first or second round of the suit to pin the ♦10.
In order to discover how to play diamonds, South should attempt to get a count on the hand. East's heart return should be won in the closed hand to preserve the ♥A as a later entry to the dummy.

South should next cash another round of trump in the closed hand, noting West's discard on the second round. South continues by cashing the ♣K, playing a club to the ♣A, and playing dummy's third club, ruffing in the closed hand.

When West follows to this trick, he is known to have started with 6 spades, 1 heart, and at least 3 clubs. West cannot have 4 diamonds and East's ♦K must be well guarded. After crossing to the ♥A, South knows enough about the distribution to lead the ♦Q from the dummy, in hopes of pinning the ♦10 in West's hand.

South next cashes the top diamonds. When West drops the ♦Q, South's extra chance has come home and the heart finesse can be taken for an overtrick.

If the ♦Q does not appear, South exits with the ♦J. If East wins the trick (so that the diamond finesse would have worked), he will be endplayed. A heart lead will remove South's possible heart loser. A spade or diamond return will concede a ruff and discard.

notes: West leads the ♠J against 6♥. West's lead is won in dummy. There is a possible loser in diamonds if the finesse is wrong. The trump suit is also a source of concern.

South should begin by taking the diamond finesse. If West wins the ♦K, South will have to play the trump suit for no losers. The only hope is a doubleton ♥Q. South should cash the ♥A and ♥K and hope for the best.

If the diamond finesse wins, South can afford a loser in trump. He should play to guard against 4 hearts to the ♥Q in West's hand. After cashing a top heart, South should continue a low heart towards dummy's ♥J. West will be unable to defeat the contract regardless of how he defends. Notice that cashing a second top honour will create a second trump loser on this lie of the cards.
Taking the diamond finesse before playing trump is an example of a discovery play. A discovery play involves testing the position in one suit (diamonds) to find out how to play another suit (hearts).

The ♣K should be cashed next and South's last club should be ruffed in dummy, eliminating clubs. South should now exit with a heart. West may be forced to win. notes: West leads the ♠10 against 6NT. West's lead is won by East with the ♠A. East returns the suit, won by South. South must hope to play the diamond suit for 4 tricks. It is necessary to assume that East has the ♦K.
If East has a singleton ♦K, South must begin the suit by cashing the ♦A. South can then finesse against West's ♦10.

If East has a doubleton ♦K, South must cross to dummy and lead a diamond honour. If East covers, South wins and can finesse against the ♦10 with West. If East ducks the first diamond lead, the ♦A will drop the ♦K on the next round.

If East has 3 diamonds to the ♦K, it is necessary to assume that West has the ♦10. East cannot gain by covering the first diamond play from dummy. Dummy's other diamond honour is then played, pinning the ♦10 in West's hand.

In order to find out how to play the diamonds, it is best to cash the other suits first (making sure to end in dummy). Three rounds of hearts show that East started with 5 hearts. A third round of spades reveals that East began with 2 spades. Finally, 3 rounds of clubs complete the count. East also began with 5 clubs and there is room for only 1 diamond in his hand. South must assume it is the ♦K and lead low to his ♦A.
If the count of the hand is not perfect, South will have to guess how many diamonds East started with.

notes: West leads the ♣Q against 6♠. The lead of the ♣Q conventionally shows the ♣J. The only possible problem is a 3-0 trump break. In this case, South must hope to engineer an endplay to avoid his club loser.

The opening lead should be won with the ♣K so that 1 of dummy's hearts can be ruffed. South should next cash the ♠A, revealing the 3-0 trump break. A second trump should be played to the ♠K and dummy's remaining heart ruffed.

South should now play diamonds. If West refuses to ruff, South should exit with a trump. West will win and he will be endplayed. A club lead will solve South's problem in that suit. A heart return will yield a ruff and discard. If West had ruffed one of the diamonds, he would have been similarily endplayed.

If East is the defender with 3 trumps, South should play along similar lines, but he should cash the ♣A early. South must hope that East began with only 2 clubs. When East is eventually thrown in with his trump trick, he will have to concede a ruff and discard.

notes: West leads the ♥5 against 4♥. The trump lead seems like a good start for the defense. South has a certain club loser. South may also have to lose 3 diamond tricks.

It seems natural for South to win the lead in the dummy and play a diamond towards the ♦K. If West can win the ♦A, the contract will almost certainly fail. West will return a second trump and the defense will arrange for the player with the third trump to win the next diamond trick.

South can improve this plan by winning the first heart in hand and immediately ducking a diamond. The trump continuation should be won in dummy for a second diamond play. If the ♦K loses to the ♦A with West, he may have no trumps to return. South will be able to ruff his diamond loser in the dummy.

South will still succeed by playing this way if East has the ♦A (although he will be sacrificing an overtrick). South can afford to lose 2 diamond tricks. By playing as suggested, South maximizes his chances of not losing 3 tricks in diamonds.

review.hl: NC5 NC4 NC3 SCA SCK SC2

notes: West leads the ♣10 against 6♠. West's lead is won in the closed hand. If trumps are 2-1, the contract will basically depend on either the heart finesse or the diamond finesse working.

If the defense has a trump trick, it appears at first glance that both the heart finesse and the diamond finesse are required. Depending on which defender has a trump trick, only one finesse is actually necessary.

If, for example, South cashes the ♠A and East discards, only the diamond finesse is needed. South should finesse the ♦Q and cash the ♦A. The ♠K is played next. South should then play clubs. If West refuses to ruff in, he is put on lead with his trump trick. West must either lead a heart into South's tenace or a diamond conceding a ruff and discard.

If West discards when the ♠A is cashed, only the heart finesse is required. A second trump is played to the ♠K and the heart finesse is taken. The ♥A is cashed and the clubs are run. East is eventually endplayed with his trump trick. He must either lead a diamond into dummy's tenace or a heart conceding a ruff and discard.

notes: West leads the ♠7 against 3NT. South's only hope is that West's lead is away from the ♠K. The ♠3 is played from dummy and South wins the ♠Q. South must hope to establish the clubs, but he can only afford to lose the lead once. The defense will always have at least 1 club trick. South should try to maximize his chances of losing only 1 club trick.

South begins by ducking the first round of clubs. The defense wins and continues spades, won in dummy. A second round of clubs is played from dummy. When East follows with a club other than the ♣K, South must decide whether to play the ♣A or the ♣Q.

Playing the ♣A will be right when East began with 3 small clubs. Playing the ♣Q will be right when East began with 3 clubs to the ♣K. As the ♣K is more likely to be with length than with shortness, South should finesse the ♣Q.

review.hl: SCA SCQ SC5 SC4 SC3 SC2
NC7 NC6 SCA SCQ SC5 SC4 SC3 SC2

notes: West leads the ♥9 against 3NT. West's lead is in response to his partner's opening bid. South should be able to come to 9 tricks via 2 spade tricks, 1 heart trick, at least 5 diamond tricks, and the ♣A. However, if the defense has a trick in diamonds, there is a danger that they will be able to take 5 tricks before South takes 9.

If a low heart is played from dummy at trick 1, East will duck. If South wins the ♥K and West has another heart and the guarded ♦K, the defense will take 4 hearts and the ♦K. If South ducks the opening lead in hand, West will switch to spades or clubs and the contract will be in trouble.

South should thus play the ♥Q from dummy at trick 1. East must win the ♥A (or South will have a second heart stopper). If East switches to a high club, South should allow him to hold the trick (or the defense might be able to take the ♥A, the ♦K, and 3 club tricks).

East will switch back to hearts. South can win the ♥K as East's opening bid showed 5 or more hearts. South crosses to the ♠K and finesses diamonds into West. West can win the ♦K, but he will be out of hearts. The ♠A and ♣A still stop the other two suits and South has 9 certain tricks.
